title: The Mexican Revolution (1884–1940)
summary: The Porfiriato and its discontents, the armed revolution of 1910–1920, the 1917 Constitution and how Calles and Cárdenas rebuilt the Mexican state.

keyterms.definition: The rule of Porfirio Díaz (1876–1880, 1884–1911), marked by order, foreign investment and growing inequality.
Technocratic advisers to Díaz who promoted positivist, 'scientific' modernisation.
Francisco Madero's 1910 call to revolt against Díaz under the slogan 'effective suffrage, no re-election'.
Emiliano Zapata's 1911 programme demanding the return of land to villages, issued in rebellion against Madero.
Forces led by Venustiano Carranza from 1913 against Huerta, including Obregón and (until 1914) Villa.
Revolutionary constitution with articles on secular education (3), land and subsoil rights (27), labour (123) and the Church (130).
Communal landholding granted to villages; expanded greatly under Cárdenas.
1926–29 Catholic rebellion against Calles' enforcement of anticlerical laws.
National Revolutionary Party founded by Calles in 1929, ancestor of the PRI, which ruled Mexico for most of the century.
Cárdenas' nationalisation of foreign oil companies on 18 March 1938, creating PEMEX.

questions.prompt: Which was a major source of discontent under the Porfiriato?
options: Concentration of land in haciendas and foreign ownership of resources
questions.explanation: Villages lost communal land, while foreign companies controlled railways, mines and oil.

questions.text: Díaz's technocratic advisers were known as the ___.
questions.explanation: The rurales were his rural police; the científicos shaped economic policy.

questions.statement: In a 1908 interview with journalist James Creelman, Díaz suggested Mexico was ready for democracy.
questions.explanation: The interview encouraged opposition such as Madero's anti-re-electionist campaign, though Díaz then ran again in 1910.

pairs.right: Commander of the Division of the North

questions.explanation: The revolutionaries united against Huerta but then fought each other.

questions.prompt: Why did Zapata turn against Madero in 1911?
options: Madero failed to return land to the villages quickly
questions.explanation: Madero was a liberal landowner focused on political reform, not land redistribution.

questions.text: Obregón defeated Villa decisively at the battles of ___ in 1915.
questions.explanation: Obregón used trenches and machine guns, lessons from the European war, against Villa's cavalry.

questions.statement: US forces occupied Veracruz in 1914 and launched a punitive expedition after Villa raided Columbus, New Mexico, in 1916.
questions.explanation: General Pershing's expedition failed to catch Villa and was withdrawn in early 1917.

questions.prompt: Which article of the 1917 Constitution gave the nation ownership of land and subsoil resources?
questions.explanation: Article 27 was the legal basis for land reform and the later oil expropriation.

questions.prompt: What happened to Zapata in 1919 and Carranza in 1920?
options: Both went into exile in the USA
questions.explanation: Zapata was ambushed by Carranza's forces; Carranza was killed fleeing Obregón's revolt.

lessons.title: Rebuilding the state: Obregón to Cárdenas (1920–1940)

questions.prompt: Which cultural programme flourished under Obregón's education minister José Vasconcelos?
options: Rural schools and public murals by artists such as Diego Rivera
questions.explanation: Muralism promoted a nationalist, revolutionary identity celebrating Mexico's indigenous past.

questions.text: The 1926–29 Catholic rebellion against Calles is called the ___ War.
questions.explanation: It ended with a US-mediated compromise in 1929.

questions.statement: The period 1928–1934, when Calles dominated presidents from behind the scenes, is called the Maximato.
questions.explanation: Calles was known as the 'Jefe Máximo'; he founded the PNR in 1929.

questions.prompt: Put these events in chronological order.
How did Cárdenas break Calles' influence?
options: He built support among workers and peasants and exiled Calles in 1936
questions.explanation: Cárdenas backed strikes, the new CTM labour confederation and land reform to build his own base.

questions.text: Cárdenas distributed land mainly as communal ___.
questions.explanation: He redistributed more land than all previous revolutionary presidents combined.

questions.prompt: Match each president to a key action.
questions.explanation: Each leader shaped the revolution's legacy differently.

questions.statement: The USA invaded Mexico in response to the 1938 oil expropriation.
questions.explanation: Roosevelt's Good Neighbor Policy and fears of war in Europe led to negotiated compensation instead.

questions.prompt: What did Cárdenas' 1938 reorganisation of the ruling party (as the PRM) do?
options: Organised it into sectors representing workers, peasants, the military and the popular classes
Gave power back to the Church
questions.explanation: This corporatist structure helped the party control Mexican politics for decades.

questions.prompt: Which is a common historiographical question about the Mexican Revolution?
options: Whether it was a genuine social revolution or a change of elites that rebuilt a strong state
Whether it happened in the 19th century
Whether it was led by the Church
questions.explanation: Revisionists stress continuity with the Porfiriato; others, like Alan Knight, emphasise popular, agrarian forces.
